---
title: "6. Candidate edits"
---

From a node with formation σ at pose χ, `Cand.legal_ops` lists the edits the
search may hand to the solver. There are 24 makes (set one bit), 24 breaks
(clear one bit), and one transport (keep σ and move). An edit to σ′ is legal
when

- it changes the formation (σ′ ≠ σ),
- **Hold**: the contacts that persist, σ ∩ σ′, pass Supported at χ (step 5), and
- **Near**: every added template has gap < `phi_gate` = 0.125 at χ.

Transport is always legal. All 48 make/break checks run in one `vmap`.

```bash
python walkthrough/06_candidates.py
```

<details><summary>The script, <code>06_candidates.py</code> (<a href="scripts/06_candidates.py">download</a>)</summary>

```python
"""Step 6: candidate edits (Cand.legal_ops).

From a node's formation, every single-bit make and break is a candidate,
plus one transport (no change). A make or break is legal when it changes
the formation, the persisting contacts pass Supported (Hold), and every
added template is within phi_gate (Near). Print the legal edits at three
fixtures.
"""
import time

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np

from cmg.marking.candidate import Cand

from _common import fixtures, load_spec, on, template_names

spec = load_spec()
cand = Cand.from_spec(spec)
names = template_names(spec, cand.catalog)
n = len(names)
legal_ops = jax.jit(lambda q: cand.legal_ops(config=q))

for fixture in ("flat", "flat_stable_close", "toppled30_close"):
    qpos = jnp.array(fixtures()[fixture])
    start = time.perf_counter()
    ops, types = legal_ops(qpos)
    ops = np.asarray(ops)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
    formation = cand.catalog.band(config=qpos)
    print(f"== {fixture}  ({elapsed:.1f} s)")
    print("  formation:", on(formation, names))
    print("  make: ", on(ops[:n], names))
    print("  break:", on(ops[n:2 * n], names))
    print("  transport:", bool(ops[2 * n]))
```

</details>

The first call compiles (about 22 s); later calls are fast.

## What to notice

- **Makes are cheap to admit.** A make keeps every current contact, so its
  hold test is just "is the current formation supported", and Near is a
  distance threshold. At `flat` 16 of the 19 unset bits pass.
- **Near admits geometric nonsense.** `B:zp-L` (the box's *top* face onto the
  floor) is legal at `flat`: its gap, 0.125, is just under `phi_gate` (the
  kernels subtract about 1e−6). So are the disk on the box's ±y faces, which
  the disk cannot reach because it never moves in y. The solver must reject
  each of them, one expensive call at a time (steps 7 and 8).
- **Breaks are where Hold bites.** At `flat` only 3 of the 5 floor bits may
  be cleared; see exercise 6.2.
- **No exclusion is checked**, because `Cand` never consults the contact graph
  (step 4).
- **The formation is recomputed from the band** when none is supplied, as here.
  Inside the search, a node's stored formation is used instead.

## Code to read

`src/cmg/marking/candidate.py`: `Cand.legal_ops`, `Cand.near`, `Cand.hold`
(the keep-set is `new_formation & old_formation`, which is the persistent-contact
rule of Decision 7, bit for bit), `Cand._hold_and_new` (the σ′ ≠ σ check), and
`Cand.apply_op` (how an operation index becomes a formation).

## Exercises

**6.1** Why is making `M:boundary-B:xp` illegal at `flat`?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

Near fails: its gap is 0.14687 (step 2), above `phi_gate` = 0.125. The disk
would have to travel around the box to reach its front face.
:::

**6.2** At `flat`, why are exactly `B:xn-L`, `B:yn-L` and `B:zn-L` breakable,
and not `B:xp-L` or `B:yp-L`?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

Use the midpoints from exercise 5.1. `B:xn-L`, `B:yn-L` and `B:zn-L` all sit
at the same corner (−0.1625, −0.0625), so clearing any one of them leaves
the same three distinct support points, and the box stays (marginally)
supported. `B:xp-L` is the only contact at (−0.0375, −0.0625), and `B:yp-L`
the only one at (−0.1625, 0.0625). Clearing either leaves two support
points, and the box cannot be balanced on them. Which bits may be dropped is
decided by which corner the closest-point routine happens to pick, not by the
physics.
:::

**6.3** At `toppled30_close`, why is breaking `M:boundary-B:xn` illegal, and
why is making `B:xn-L` legal?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

The break would leave only environment contacts, and those fail EnvStable
there (step 5): the box would fall back. The make keeps every current contact,
which is supported, and the box's −x face is within 0.125 of the floor
because the box is tilted only 30°. Hold says nothing about whether the
make can be *realized*; that is the solver's job.
:::
